as a backdrop, Secretary Rubio says the world has much to learn from the men of ancient Greece,
who knew there was nothing selfish about fighting for their own interests. But he says nationalism
has become a dirty word, and now the West is at a crossroads. The course we take will determine

of drone warfare, critical minerals and artificial intelligence, which Trump is trying to rebrand

the State Department. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for
international students who are seeking to work in the U.S. It's the latest effort from the Trump
administration to crack down on foreign enrollment. The change would represent a blow to American
colleges and universities that heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition
revenue. The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal. Support for Medicare for All is the
highest it's been in at least a decade, according to New Polling Kate Wells with our partner KFF
Health News reports. If you go to one of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El Sayed's town halls in
Michigan, you will hear the crowd chant the campaign slogan. Two in three Americans now
say they favor Medicare for All, according to polling from KFF, a health policy research
organization. But many of them don't actually know what it means and that support fluctuates
based on what pollsters told them about it. Medicare for All usually means a single insurance
program run by the federal government that replaces or radically changes private insurance.
Opponents argue that Medicare for All would raise taxes and could lead to treatment delays.
That's Kate Wells with our partner KFF Health News. The FCC is considering a request to loosen
rules on political robocalls, including those with A.I.-generated voices. Current federal laws
banned most robocalls to cell phones. A conservative group called Club for Growth
is seeking the change, arguing it could improve voter communication and polling accuracy.
Consumer advocacy groups warned the change could lead to a surge of unwanted
and misleading calls before the midterm elections. This is NPR News.
Nearly a month after President Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill named after Lindsey Graham,
Senate leaders in both parties are urging the administration to use the new law to help Ukraine
and a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Besant and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The senators say they want the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on the flow of money
fueling Russia's war, especially the shadow fleet of tankers Moscow is using to transport oil.
A new study finds that modern indigenous populations share many ancient microbes
that most of the world is missing, and Piers Ping Huang reports.
The Hadza people of Tanzania and the Chamani people of Bolivia lived thousands of miles
in an ocean apart, yet researchers compared their gut bacteria and found they had 90 percent of the
same species in their digestive tracts. Justin Sonnenberg at Stanford University is senior author
on the paper. These populations in South America and in Africa and probably in other parts of the
world are transmitting microbes over generations. The similarities in their gut bacteria are
remarkable. Sonnenberg and his colleagues found that most of these bacteria are missing in modern
industrialized people, which raises questions like whether losing these microbial species
could affect susceptibility to chronic and inflammatory diseases such as certain
cancers or diabetes. The paper is published in the journal Nature, Ping Huang, NPR News.
There's a race to the bottom of the NFL standings four games into the season,
a record-tying five teams have no wins one month in,
marking just the seventh time that's happened in NFL history and the first time since 2019.
